sourceCourseTitle: Llm Application Security Red Teaming Specialist / Threat Modeling for LLM Apps

body.en:
In this lesson you will learn:

- 1) How to enumerate components and trust boundaries in an LLM application (models, prompts, tools, RAG, data stores, and third-party services)

- 2) How to map data and capability flows to identify abuse paths like prompt injection → tool misuse → data exfiltration

- 3) How to prioritize mitigations and document a defensible threat model that guides testing and verification.

blocks.title: AI Model Penetration: Testing LLMs for Prompt Injection
blocks.label: Course Video

body.en:
An LLM app’s attack surface spans inputs (user prompts, uploaded files, retrieved web/content, system prompts), orchestration (agents, function calling, tool routers), and side-effecting sinks (code execution, file I/O, HTTP calls, DB writes, email/transactions, UI rendering).

Map trust boundaries where untrusted content crosses into privileged capabilities—especially RAG pipelines, tool/agent layers, and third-party APIs.

Common threats include direct/indirect prompt injection, insecure output handling (HTML/JS/SQL/shell injection), tool abuse and over-privilege, data exfiltration via connectors, training data poisoning, model denial of service (token/cost abuse), and logging/telemetry leaks.

Effective mapping uses an asset inventory, data flow diagrams with sources/sinks, capability inventories for tools, and attack trees to enumerate misuse paths.

Mitigations include allowlists and schema validation for tools, least privilege and scoped credentials, sandboxing and time/network/file guards, robust input/output filters, provenance checks in RAG, and continuous red-teaming with safety/eval gates.

• Trust boundaries and data/capability flows: Identify where untrusted content enters and which sinks can cause side effects.
• Tool/agent capability surface: Enumerate tools, required privileges, argument schemas, and guardrails; apply least privilege and approvals.
• Untrusted inputs beyond the chat box: Treat retrieved pages, PDFs, plugin responses, and prior model outputs as tainted and validate before use.

question.en: Your RAG chatbot can browse the web and write files via a filesystem tool. Which trust boundary is the highest priority to harden to prevent indirect prompt injection leading to file writes?

text.en: Between the UI and API gateway
Between external web content and the tool invocation layer
Between the vector store and the embedding model
Between the observability exporter and the SIEM

explanation.en: Untrusted web content can steer the model to invoke tools. Harden the content→LLM→tool path with allowlists, schema/regex validation, and sandboxed file I/O.

question.en: Which control most directly reduces the risk of malicious retrieved content triggering dangerous tool calls?

text.en: Increase model temperature
Tool allowlist with strict argument validation, least-privilege credentials, and human approval for high-impact actions
Use a larger foundation model
Strengthen the system prompt only

explanation.en: Capability controls (allowlist, validation, privilege scoping, approvals) constrain effects even if the model is influenced; prompt-only defenses are insufficient.

question.en: Which artifact best captures an LLM app’s attack surface for security review and testing?

text.en: Organization chart
Data flow diagram showing sources/sinks, trust boundaries, tools, and third-party services
Sprint backlog
UI wireframes

explanation.en: A detailed DFD with trust boundaries and side-effecting sinks enables systematic threat enumeration and test planning.

body.en:
• Treat all retrieved/generated text as untrusted when it can influence tools, code, or rendering.
• Map tools and side-effecting sinks first; apply least privilege, allowlists, schema/regex guards, and sandboxing.
• Use DFDs, attack trees, and continuous red-teaming/evals to keep the threat model current as capabilities change.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand the core concepts and can apply them in practice.

In this lesson you will learn: 1) The major OWASP LLM Top 10 risk areas and why they matter 2) How to recognize common attack scenarios and failure modes in LLM apps 3) How to apply layered mitigations, testing, and governance aligned to these categories.

The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications catalogs the most impactful risks observed in real systems. As of 2024, the public list (2023) highlights areas such as prompt injection (including indirect), insecure output handling, training data poisoning, model denial of service (token/cost abuse), supply chain vulnerabilities, sensitive information disclosure, insecure plugin/tool design, excessive agency, and overreliance on LLMs; many discussions also include model theft/extraction.

A 2025-focused view emphasizes agents/tools, retrieval (RAG) safety and provenance, tighter capability bounding, and continuous evaluation. Mitigations pair technical controls (input/output filters, schema validation, sandboxing, rate limits/budgets, provenance and content moderation, SBOMs and dependency review) with process controls (least privilege, approvals for high-risk actions, red-teaming, and incident response). Effective adoption maps each OWASP category to specific architecture components, test cases, and monitoring signals.

blocks.title: Stop Prompt Injection, Guardrail Bypass & Output Leakage
blocks.label: Recommended Viewing

body.en:
• Prompt injection (direct and indirect): Untrusted content can steer models and tools; lexical filtering alone is insufficient—constrain capabilities and validate arguments.
• Insecure output handling: Model output rendered or executed without sanitization/escaping enables HTML/JS/SQL/shell injection—use safe parsers, sandboxes, and strict content types.
• Supply chain and plugin/tool security: Review models, gateways, and plugins; maintain SBOMs, pin versions, scope secrets, and implement least-privilege, allowlists, and approvals.

question.en: Your app renders LLM-generated HTML snippets inside an internal dashboard without sanitization. Which OWASP LLM risk does this most directly represent?

text.en: Prompt Injection
Insecure Output Handling
Supply Chain Vulnerabilities
Excessive Agency

explanation.en: Unsafely rendering model output is an output-handling issue that can enable XSS and similar injection, regardless of how the prompt was formed.

question.en: A plugin allows sending emails and creating tickets. To align with OWASP guidance, which approach best reduces the combined risk of Insecure Plugin Design and Excessive Agency?

text.en: Increase the model’s temperature to encourage diverse outputs
Disable all logs to reduce information exposure
Enforce least-privilege scopes, strict schema validation, allowlists, and require explicit user approval for high-impact actions
Use a larger context window so the model sees more policy text

explanation.en: Capability bounding with validation and approvals constrains real-world side effects even if the model makes mistakes or is influenced.

question.en: User prompts sometimes include API keys that end up stored in logs and analytics. Which OWASP LLM category does this most directly map to?

text.en: Model Denial of Service
Sensitive Information Disclosure
Training Data Poisoning
Overreliance on LLMs

explanation.en: Secrets in prompts being persisted or exposed through logs/telemetry is a sensitive information disclosure risk; apply redaction, data minimization, and access controls.

body.en:
• Map OWASP LLM risks to concrete components: inputs, retrieval, tools/agents, sinks, and monitoring.
• Combine guardrails: constrain capabilities, validate inputs/outputs, sanitize/sandbox, and rate limit/budget.
• Verify continuously with red-teaming and evals; enforce governance via SBOMs, reviews, and least-privilege access.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand the core concepts and can apply them in practice.

title.en: Data flows, trust boundaries and tool permissions

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How to map end-to-end data flows for LLM applications, including prompts, context retrieval, and tool calls
- 2) How to identify and validate trust boundaries where identities, networks, or privilege levels change
- 3) How to design and enforce least-privilege tool permissions, with scoping, egress controls, and auditing

Modern LLM applications involve multiple moving parts: the client (web/mobile), API gateway and auth, an orchestrator/agent, prompt construction and policy filters, a vector database or other retrieval stores (RAG), the LLM provider (self-hosted or SaaS), and external tools (plugins, APIs, databases, code execution sandboxes). Mapping data flows means tracing how data moves among these components: user input → preprocessing/redaction → embedding/indexing (for ingestion) → retrieval → prompt assembly (system + developer + user + context) → model inference → tool invocation(s) → post-processing → response, while also capturing logging/telemetry and storage of artifacts.

Identify data types (e.g., public, internal, secrets, PII) and mark where each is processed or persisted. Trust boundaries are points where trust assumptions change, such as: user device → your frontend; frontend → backend; your network → third-party model provider; your orchestrator → external tools; tenant A → tenant B; human-in-the-loop review; browser sandbox → server; online → offline batch.

Each boundary requires authentication, authorization, input validation, output handling, and monitoring. For LLMs, prompt injection often attempts to cross these boundaries by coercing the agent to exfiltrate data or invoke tools outside intent, so treat model outputs as untrusted until validated.

Tool permissions govern what an LLM agent can do when calling tools. Apply least privilege with: capability scoping (only the minimal tools), resource scoping (per-tenant/database/collection), allowlists for hosts/endpoints, argument schemas with strict validation, rate/egress limits, time-bound and context-bound credentials, and human approval for high-risk actions (e.g., financial transactions, code deployment).

Use isolation for risky tools (network sandbox, read-only FS), secrets segmentation (per-tool tokens), signed tool invocations, and audit logs that capture who/what/when/why. Align with policy-as-code to enforce constraints consistently across environments.

• Data Flow Diagram (DFD): Visual map of external entities, processes, data stores, and data flows that reveals where controls are needed
• Trust Boundary: A point where identity, privilege, or network isolation changes and where validation, authentication, and authorization must occur
• Tool Permission Scoping: Restricting tool capabilities by action, data scope, time, and network egress to contain prompt-injection and tool-abuse risks

question.en: Your LLM agent can use web_browse and sql_query tools. Both currently share one long-lived API key and have unrestricted outbound network access. Users can paste arbitrary URLs. Which change most reduces the risk of cross-tenant data exfiltration if a prompt injection triggers both tools?

text.en: Add more toxicity filtering to the model’s output
Issue per-tenant, time-scoped credentials and enforce an allowlist for outbound hosts and SQL roles
Increase the model’s temperature to reduce repetitive outputs
Aggregate logs into a single dashboard without changing configs

explanation.en: Per-tenant, time-scoped credentials and egress allowlisting implement least privilege across trust boundaries, limiting what an injected flow can access or exfiltrate.

question.en: Where is a trust boundary that most requires explicit validation in an LLM app using third-party plugins?

text.en: Between two mTLS-authenticated microservices within the same service identity and VPC
Between the system prompt and the user prompt inside the orchestrator
Between your orchestrator and a third-party plugin marketplace/API
Between the vector store and the embedding worker on the same private subnet

explanation.en: Cross-organization and cross-identity calls to third-party plugins cross a strong trust boundary and require authentication, authorization, schema validation, and output handling.

question.en: For a RAG chatbot, what is the best first step when documenting data flows?

text.en: Identify external entities, assets, and stores, then sketch a DFD before enumerating threats
Start with a penetration test and only document findings afterwards
List mitigations and controls before understanding how data moves
Finalize SLAs with stakeholders before mapping the system

explanation.en: Start with scope and a DFD so you understand assets and flows; then assess threats and select controls informed by that map.

body.en:
• Map all prompt, retrieval, tool, and logging flows to see where sensitive data moves
• Treat LLM outputs and tool responses as untrusted across trust boundaries; validate and constrain them
• Enforce least-privilege tool permissions with scoped credentials, allowlists, argument validation, and auditing
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how to chart data flows, locate trust boundaries, and apply least-privilege tool permissions in LLM applications.

blocks.title: Guardrails for LLM Applications | Complete Tutorial for AI Developers
blocks.label: Tutorial

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to structure clear, complete threat model documentation for LLM applications 2) How to capture scope, assumptions, DFDs, trust boundaries, and a tool-permission matrix 3) How to record risks, controls, and validation plans as a living, versioned artifact

Effective threat model documentation explains how and why the system is secure, and how it will be tested. Core sections include: scope and objectives; assumptions and out-of-scope; architecture overview with data flow diagrams (DFDs) and trust boundaries; data classification (PII, secrets, internal); assets and external entities; entry points; misuse/abuse cases; threat enumeration (e.g., STRIDE for integrity/availability/spoofing risks and LINDDUN for privacy; plus LLM-specific issues like prompt injection, tool abuse, data leakage, model supply chain, and training data poisoning); risk rating (likelihood × impact with clear criteria); mitigations mapped to controls and owners; residual risk with sign-off; and a verification plan (red-team scenarios, automated tests, canary prompts, tool invocation tests, egress checks).

For LLM apps, document prompt channels (system, developer, user), safety policies, content filters, and the tool-permission matrix: for each tool, define allowed actions, scopes (tenant/db/collection/host allowlist), auth method, rate/egress limits, approval requirements, and audit fields. Make it a living document: store in version control, link to architecture-as-code and IaC, update on every material change (new tool, new data store, new provider), and include a change log.

Use templates or tools (e.g., OWASP Threat Dragon, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool, IriusRisk) to standardize content and export diagrams. Tie each risk to verification artifacts (test cases, monitors, SLOs) to ensure controls are effective and regressions are caught.

• Threat Model Template: Standard sections (scope, assumptions, DFDs, risks, controls, verification) ensure consistency and coverage
• Tool Permission Matrix: A table capturing each tool’s actions, scope, auth, egress limits, approval, and audit fields for LLM agents
• Verification Traceability: Each identified risk links to specific tests, monitors, and owners, enabling continuous validation and audits

question.en: Which addition most improves the clarity and reuse of an LLM app’s threat model document?

text.en: A long narrative description of the system without diagrams
A versioned template with DFDs, explicit assumptions, and a tool-permission matrix
An appendix listing all CVEs published this year
A separate legal memo stored outside the repository

explanation.en: Templates plus DFDs and explicit assumptions create consistent, maintainable, and auditable documentation; the tool-permission matrix addresses LLM-specific risks.

question.en: Your team adds a new third-party plugin that executes code to transform files. What should be updated in the threat model documentation first?

text.en: The product logo in the cover page
Only the system prompt text
The DFD, trust boundaries, tool-permission matrix, and risks/tests for code execution and egress
Wait for the next annual audit before changing the document

explanation.en: Material changes require updating diagrams, boundaries, permissions, and associated risks and verification to preserve accuracy and traceability.

question.en: What is the best way to capture residual risk decisions in an LLM threat model?

text.en: Record explicit sign-off with risk owner, rationale, compensating controls, and review/expiry date
Keep notes in team chat so they are informal and flexible
Remove the risk from the register to reduce noise
Postpone documentation until after release

explanation.en: Residual risk needs documented ownership, rationale, and time-bound review to satisfy governance and enable re-evaluation as the system evolves.

body.en:
• A good threat model is a living, version-controlled document with clear scope, DFDs, and explicit assumptions
• LLM-specific sections (prompt channels, safety policies, tool-permission matrix) make risks and controls concrete
• Link every risk to controls, owners, and tests to ensure continuous verification and auditability
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now create and maintain effective, auditable threat model documentation for LLM applications.
